chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Behavioral Economics Is (and Isn't)

lessons.title: Bounded Rationality: Why Rational Economic Man Never Existed

children.text: Vikram, a 29-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru, opens an investing app to pick his first mutual fund. India has more than 40 AMCs offering over 1,500 schemes across categories. After twenty minutes of scrolling, he picks whichever large-cap fund shows the highest 3-year return at the top of the list and stops looking. Was Vikram being lazy or irrational? Herbert Simon, the economist who coined the term this lesson is named after, would say no. Vikram did exactly what a real human being with real limits is supposed to do.

body.text: People don't optimize across infinite information. They satisfice: they stop searching once they find an option that is good enough, because gathering and processing more information costs real time and effort. This is not a flaw to be corrected. It is rational behavior given the real limits every human decision maker faces.

children.text: The Man Who Broke Homo Economicus, Decades Before Kahneman

markDefs.definition: The idea, introduced by Herbert Simon, that human decision-making is constrained by incomplete information, limited mental processing power, and limited time, so people cannot actually optimize the way classical economic models assume.

children.text: Herbert Simon, an economist, political scientist and one of the founders of artificial intelligence research, coined the term
bounded rationality

in a 1955 paper called "A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice." He won the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for it, twenty-four years before Kahneman's Nobel and thirty-nine years before Thaler's. Simon's argument was simple and hard to dispute: homo economicus assumes a decision maker who knows every option, can process unlimited information instantly at no cost, and always picks the single best one. No real person, and no real organization, works that way.
Simon pointed to three limits that box in every real decision, whether it is Vikram picking a mutual fund or a bank approving a loan:
Incomplete information.
Nobody has ever read the offer documents of all 1,500-plus mutual fund schemes in India, and nobody ever will.
Limited processing power.
Even with perfect information, no human brain can hold 1,500 risk-return profiles in working memory and compare them all at once.
Limited time.
A decision has to get made. Vikram has a life to run, and an infinite search for the perfect fund has a real cost: every day undecided is a day his money sits idle.

columns.label: Homo economicus (the model)
points: Has complete information about every option
Processes unlimited information instantly, at zero cost
Always chooses the single mathematically optimal option
Never runs out of time, attention, or energy

columns.label: The boundedly rational decision maker (reality)
points: Knows only a limited subset of the available options
Has finite time, attention, and mental effort to spend on any one decision
Stops at the first option that clears a "good enough" bar
Weighs the effort of deciding against the stakes of the decision

children.text: Satisficing: Good Enough Beats Perfect

markDefs.definition: A term Herbert Simon coined by combining "satisfy" and "suffice." It means stopping the search at the first option that clears an acceptable threshold, rather than continuing to search for the mathematically optimal one.

children.text: In a 1956 paper, Simon gave this behavior a name:
satisficing

. Vikram did not maximize, he satisficed: he set an acceptable bar, in his case a fund with a strong recent track record from a familiar-sounding AMC, and stopped as soon as an option cleared it. Given that reviewing every scheme properly would take far longer than the decision is worth, satisficing is not second-best behavior. It is often the only sensible strategy available.

body.title: Why nobody reviews every scheme
body.prompt: If Vikram spent a careful 10 minutes properly evaluating each of India's roughly 1,500 mutual fund schemes before deciding, how many hours would that take in total?
body.explanation: 1,500 schemes × 10 minutes = 15,000 minutes, or 250 hours. That is over 31 working days of 8 hours each spent only on research, before a single rupee is invested. This is precisely why satisficing, not optimizing, is the only realistic approach for an individual investor.

children.text: Institutions Are Boundedly Rational Too

Bounded rationality is not just a private, individual problem. Regulators and lenders face the exact same limits at a larger scale, and several familiar Indian financial-market features exist specifically to help boundedly rational people satisfice safely rather than pretend they can optimize.

cells: Investors cannot individually evaluate the risk of 1,500-plus schemes
Mandatory colour-coded Riskometer on every scheme, and a 2017 scheme-categorisation rule limiting each AMC to one scheme per category
Health insurance policies vary too much in wording to compare quickly
Arogya Sanjeevani Policy, a standard baseline product launched in 2020 so any two insurers' offerings can be compared apples to apples
A loan officer cannot deeply investigate every borrower's full financial history
A single CIBIL credit score used as a fast, good-enough proxy for creditworthiness

body.text: Notice what all three fixes have in common: none of them make more information available. They make the information easier to satisfice on. A five-level Riskometer is objectively less precise than reading a scheme's full portfolio, but far more usable, because usability, not precision, is what a boundedly rational decision maker actually needs.

children.text: Two Schools Within Behavioral Economics

Simon's bounded rationality and Kahneman and Tversky's later heuristics-and-biases program, the paper you met in the previous lesson, both dismantle homo economicus, but for different reasons. Simon's decision maker is still trying to be rational; he is simply blocked by real constraints of information, computing power and time, and satisficing is his sensible response to those constraints. Kahneman and Tversky's decision maker often has enough time and information, yet still deviates from rational choice in a predictable direction, because the brain's shortcuts, or heuristics, misfire in specific, repeatable ways even when the constraints Simon described are not binding. This course draws on both traditions: some chapters explain behavior through limits on information and time, others through the specific mental shortcuts covered starting in the next lesson.

body.title: Which explanation fits which school
body.question: Priya compares only three term insurance quotes out of 25 available insurers before buying the one that fits her budget. Which explanation best fits Herbert Simon's specific concept of bounded rationality, rather than a later heuristics-and-biases explanation?
options: Priya is anchored on the very first quote she saw and cannot mentally move far from it
Priya has limited time and effort to spend on this decision, so she satisfices at a good-enough option rather than searching exhaustively
Priya is overconfident that her quote is definitely the cheapest one available
Priya bought what her colleagues recently bought, a form of herd behavior
body.explanation: Option B is a direct description of satisficing under real time and effort constraints, exactly what Simon's bounded rationality predicts. The other three options describe specific cognitive biases, anchoring, overconfidence, and herd behavior, which belong to the heuristics-and-biases tradition covered elsewhere in this course.

body.title: Name the strategy
body.textWithBlank: Herbert Simon used the word ___ to describe stopping the search at the first option that clears a good-enough bar, rather than continuing to search for the mathematically optimal one.
body.explanation: Satisficing blends "satisfy" and "suffice." It is Simon's name for rational decision-making under real limits on information, cognitive effort, and time.

body.title: Was Herbert Simon an economist, a psychologist, or something else?

children.text: All three, and more. Simon earned his PhD in political science from the University of Chicago in 1943, spent his career at Carnegie Mellon University, and in 1956 co-created the Logic Theorist with Allen Newell and Cliff Shaw, widely considered one of the first artificial intelligence programs ever built. He won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1978 without ever holding an economics degree, because his research into how decisions actually get made inside organizations cut across psychology, computer science, and economics all at once. Bounded rationality was born from that cross-disciplinary view, not from inside standard economics.

body.label: Herbert Simon's 1978 Nobel Prize Facts Page
body.description: A short official summary of why Herbert Simon won the prize, decades before behavioral economics became mainstream.

body.label: The first Nobel to challenge homo economicus
body.context: Herbert Simon's Nobel came 24 years before Kahneman's (2002) and 39 years before Thaler's (2017), for showing that real decision makers satisfice rather than optimize.

cards.definition: Herbert Simon's idea that decision-making is limited by incomplete information, limited processing power, and limited time, making true optimization impossible for real people and organizations.
Stopping the search at the first option that clears an acceptable, "good enough" bar, rather than continuing to search for the mathematically optimal one.
Economist, political scientist, and AI pioneer who coined bounded rationality (1955) and satisficing (1956), and won the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

Kahneman and Tversky's research tradition showing that people deviate from rational choice in specific, repeatable ways even when they have enough time and information, distinct from Simon's constraint-based explanation.
The practical difficulty of deciding well when the number of available options is very large, such as 1,500-plus mutual fund schemes or dozens of health insurance products.

points: Bounded rationality, coined by Herbert Simon in 1955, says decisions are constrained by incomplete information, limited processing power, and limited time, not by irrationality.
Satisficing, stopping at the first good-enough option instead of searching for the perfect one, is a rational response to those limits, not a shortcut to be ashamed of.
Simon won the Nobel Prize for this in 1978, well before Kahneman (2002) and Thaler (2017), making bounded rationality the earliest serious crack in the homo economicus model.
Institutions satisfice too. SEBI's Riskometer, IRDAI's standard health policy, and CIBIL scores all exist to make good-enough decisions faster and safer, not to enable perfect ones.

Bounded rationality and the heuristics-and-biases tradition from the previous lesson are two different explanations for why homo economicus fails: one points to real constraints, the other to specific mental shortcuts that misfire even without those constraints.
